Triggers.value: Medical equipment such as needles or drips

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I try to erase the memory of the event
constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy

Memory.value: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank

Negative Appraisals.value: My life has been destroyed by the trauma
I have failed in my most important role in life
My body has been permanently damaged by what happened

issues.item: Triggers: Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened
issues.explanation: 'Being in nature similar to where it happened' is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of life-threatening illness, which typically involves medical/health contexts rather than a natural-environment trauma setting.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
issues.explanation: 'Avoid grief reminders' implies bereavement/loss of another person, which does not fit the stated trauma type of life-threatening illness unless there is an unreported death-related trauma; it is not supported by the other selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: 'Fear of rage' is weakly connected to the rest of the profile: the other appraisals and memory items center on damage, unreality, and role failure after illness, not anger-based dyscontrol. This makes the appraisal set less internally coherent.

vignette: Leela's eyes scanned the hospital room, taking in the familiar beeps of monitors and the sterile smell that clung to every surface. It was a scent she had grown all too accustomed to during her months-long battle with leukemia. As a project manager, Leela was used to being in control, but the diagnosis had upended her life, leaving her feeling vulnerable and powerless. The memory of those days still felt like a blur, as if it had happened to someone else. There were moments that stood out with crystal clarity - the sound of the doctor's voice delivering the diagnosis, the feel of the cold hospital bed beneath her skin, the sight of needles and medical equipment surrounding her - but others were lost in a haze. Leela couldn't shake the feeling that it was all just a terrible dream, one she couldn't wake up from. As she began to recover, Leela found herself avoiding anything that might trigger those memories. She wouldn't go near hospitals or ambulances, and even avoided physical examinations with her doctor. The smell of disinfectant or the sight of medical equipment would send her spiraling back into anxiety. Her husband tried to be supportive, but Leela couldn't help feeling like she was failing him, like she had failed in her most important role as a partner. Leela's mind became preoccupied with thoughts of her own mortality and the fragility of her body. She felt like she was constantly on edge, waiting for the other shoe to drop, for the cancer to come back and destroy what little sense of security she had left. Her friends and family tried to reassure her that she was in remission, but Leela couldn't shake the feeling that her life had been irreparably damaged. As time went on, Leela began to develop a new habit - constantly monitoring her own thoughts for signs that she might be "going crazy". She would catch herself thinking about the cancer and immediately try to push the thought away, worried that dwelling on it would somehow make it come back. It was exhausting, but Leela felt like it was the only way to keep herself safe. Despite her best efforts, memories of the illness continued to surface in unexpected ways. A cold wind might blow through the office building and suddenly Leela would be transported back to those freezing hospital nights. The smell of a certain soap or perfume could evoke the same feelings of anxiety and fear that had defined those long months. And sometimes, without warning, Leela would feel the full weight of her emotions - the sadness, the anger, the fear - without any clear image or memory to anchor them. Leela's life as a project manager began to suffer as she struggled to keep up with the demands of her job while also managing her anxiety. Meetings became overwhelming, and she found herself avoiding social interactions altogether. Her relationships with colleagues and friends began to fray, and Leela felt like she was losing herself in the process. It wasn't until her husband sat her down and gently suggested that maybe it was time to seek help that Leela realized just how far things had gone. She was afraid of what therapy might uncover, but more than that, she was afraid of living the rest of her life trapped in this cycle of fear and avoidance. As she walked into the therapist's office for the first time, Leela felt a glimmer of hope - maybe, just maybe, there was a way to rebuild her shattered sense of self and learn to live with the memories that haunted her.
